¶ '''unkindship†''' (un-kīnd′ship), ''n.'' [ME. ''unkyndship''; < ''unkind'' + ''-ship''.] An unnatural act. {{smaller block|The childe his owne father slough;
That was ''unkyndship'' enough. {{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., vi.}}}} '''unking''' (un-king′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''2 + ''king''1.] To deprive of royalty. {{smaller block|They would ''unking'' my father now
To make you way. {{right|''Southern.''}}}} '''unkingly''' (un-king′li), ''a.'' Not kingly; unbecoming a king; not noble. {{smaller block|What shameful words (''unkingly'' as thou art)
Fall from that trembling tongue and tim’rous heart? {{right|''Pope'', Iliad, xiv. 90.}}}} '''unkingship†''' (un-king′ship), ''n.'' [< ''un-''1 + ''kingship''.] The state or condition of being unkinged. {{smaller block|''Un-kingship'' was proclaim’d, and his Majesty’s statues thrown down at St. Paul’s Portico and the Exchange. {{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, May 30, 1649.}}}} '''unkiss''' (un-kis′), ''v. t.'' To retract or annul by kissing again, as an oath taken by kissing the book. ''Shak.'', Rich. II., v. 1. 74. [Rare.] '''unkith''', ''a.'' Same as ''unked''. '''unknelled''' (un-neld′), ''a.'' Untolled; not having the bell tolled for one at death or funeral. ''Byron'', Childe Harold, iv. '''unknightliness''' (un-nīt′li-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unknightly. '''unknightly''' (un-nīt′li), ''a.'' Contrary to the rules of chivalry; unworthy of a knight. ''Scott'', The Talisman.

'''unknowing''' (un-nō′ing), ''p. a.'' [< ME. ''unknowyng, unknawynge''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''knowing''.] Not knowing; ignorant: with ''of'' before an object.

readings.c2s3:
{{smaller block|<poem>A mead of mildest charm delays the ''unlabouring'' feet.</poem>
{{right|''Coleridge'', To Cottle.}}}}

'''unlaborious''' (un-lā-bō′ri-us), ''a.'' Not laborious; not toilsome; not difficult; easy. ''Milton'', Areopagitica.

'''unlaboriously''' (un-lā-bō′ri-us-li), ''adv.'' In an unlaborious manner; easily.

'''unlace''' (un-lās′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''unlacen, unlasen''; < ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''lace.''] '''1.''' To loose from lacing or fastening by a cord, string, band, or the like passed through loops, holes, etc.; open or unfasten by undoing or untying the lace of: as, to ''unlace'' a garment or a helmet.
{{smaller block|However, I am not sure if they do not sometimes ''unlace'' that part of the sail from the yard.
{{right|''Cook'', Second Voyage, III. ii.}}}}
'''2.''' To loosen or ease the dress or armor of.
{{smaller block|<poem>My lorde, ''vn-lase'' you to lye,
Here schall none come for to crye.</poem>
{{right|''York Plays'', p. 293.}}}}
'''3.''' To divest of due covering; expose to injury or damage. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>What ’s the matter,
That you ''unlace'' your reputation thus?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, ii. 3. 194.}}}}
'''4.''' To disentangle.
{{smaller block|So entrelaced that it is unable to be ''unlaced.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, iii. prose 12.}}}}
'''5†.''' To carve.
{{smaller block|''Vnlace'' that cony. {{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 265.}}}}

'''unlade''' (un-lād′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''lade''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' To unload; take out the cargo of.

{{RunningHeader|unkindship|6625|unlawful}}{{nop}}'''unkindship†''' (un-kīnd′ship), ''n.'' [ME. ''unkyndship''; < ''unkind'' + ''-ship''.] An unnatural act. {{smaller block|The childe his owne father slough;
That was ''unkyndship'' enough. {{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., vi.}}}} '''unking''' (un-king′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''2 + ''king''1.] To deprive of royalty. {{smaller block|They would ''unking'' my father now
To make you way. {{right|''Southern.''}}}} '''unkingly''' (un-king′li), ''a.'' Not kingly; unbecoming a king; not noble. {{smaller block|What shameful words (''unkingly'' as thou art)
Fall from that trembling tongue and tim’rous heart? {{right|''Pope'', Iliad, xiv. 90.}}}} '''unkingship†''' (un-king′ship), ''n.'' [< ''un-''1 + ''kingship''.] The state or condition of being unkinged. {{smaller block|''Un-kingship'' was proclaim’d, and his Majesty’s statues thrown down at St. Paul’s Portico and the Exchange. {{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, May 30, 1649.}}}} '''unkiss''' (un-kis′), ''v. t.'' To retract or annul by kissing again, as an oath taken by kissing the book. ''Shak.'', Rich. II., v. 1. 74. [Rare.] '''unkith''', ''a.'' Same as ''unked''. '''unknelled''' (un-neld′), ''a.'' Untolled; not having the bell tolled for one at death or funeral. ''Byron'', Childe Harold, iv. '''unknightliness''' (un-nīt′li-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unknightly. '''unknightly''' (un-nīt′li), ''a.'' Contrary to the rules of chivalry; unworthy of a knight. ''Scott'', The Talisman. '''unknit''' (un-nit′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''unknitted'' or ''unknit'', ppr. ''unknitting''. [< ME. ''unknytten''; < ''un-''2 + ''knit''.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To untie, as a knot; unwrinkle or smooth out; undo, as knitted work. {{smaller block|The whiche ''vnknytteth'' alle care and comsyng is of reste. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xxi. 225.}} ''Unknit'' that threatening, unkind brow. {{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., v. 2. 136.}} Where they trick her [the Bride] in her richest ornaments, tying on her silken buskins with knots not easily ''unknit''. {{right|''Sandys'', Travailes, p. 52.}}}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' To become separated; relax. [Rare.] {{smaller block|Loue is so natural to man or woman, and the desire to be beloued, that where loue amongst them doeth once cleaue it is a . . . bonde that neuer ''unknitteth''. {{right|''Guevara'', Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 187.}}}} '''unknot''' (un-not′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''unknotted'', ppr. ''unknotting''. [< ''un-''2 + ''knot''1.] To free from knots; untie. '''unknotty''' (un-not′i), ''a.'' Not knotty; having no knots. ''Sandys'', tr. of Ovid’s Metamorph., x. [Rare.] '''unknow''' (un-nō′), ''v. t.''; pret. ''unknew'', pp. ''unknown'', ppr. ''unknowing''. [< ME. ''unknowen''; < ''un-''2 + ''know''1.] '''1.''' To become ignorant of, or unacquainted with, as something already known; lose the knowledge of. {{smaller block|Can I ''unknow'' it?—No, but keep it secret. {{right|''Dryden'', Duke of Guise, v. 1.}}}} '''2.''' Not to know; to have no knowledge of or acquaintance with. ''Wyclif'', Rom. i. 13. [Rare in both uses.] '''unknowability''' (un-nō-a̤-bil′i̤-ti), ''n.'' [< ''unknowable'' + ''-ity'' (see ''-bility'').] The state or character of being unknowable. ''J. S. Mill.'' '''unknowable''' (un-nō′a̤-bl), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unknowable''; < ''un-''1 + ''knowable''.] '''1.''' Incapable of being known; not capable of being ascertained or discovered; above or beyond knowledge. {{smaller block|Their objects, transcending the sphere of all experience actual or possible, consequently do not fall under the categories, in other words are positively ''unknowable.'' {{right|''Sir W. Hamilton.''}}}} {{smaller block|By continually seeking to know, and being continually thrown back with a deepened conviction of the impossibility of knowing, we may keep alive the consciousness that it is alike our highest wisdom and our highest duty to regard that through which all things exist as The ''Unknowable.'' {{right|''H. Spencer'', First Principles, § 31.}}}} '''2†.''' Unknown. {{smaller block|Liggeth thanne stille al owtrely ''unknowable.'' {{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, ii. meter 7.}}}} '''unknowableness''' (un-nō′a̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unknowable. {{smaller block|Herbert Spencer insists on the certainty of the existence of things in themselves, but also on their absolute and eternal ''unknowableness.'' {{right|''J. F. Clarke'', Orthodoxy, p. 25.}}}} '''unknowably''' (un-nō′a̤-bli), ''adv.'' Not so as to be known. '''unknowe†''', ''a.'' A Middle English form of ''unknown''. '''unknowing''' (un-nō′ing), ''p. a.'' [< ME. ''unknowyng, unknawynge''; < ''un-''1 + ''knowing''.] Not knowing; ignorant: with ''of'' before an object. 416 {{smaller block|Butte vppe they rose, to say yow ferthermore, And chaungyd horses onto them bothe ''vnknowyng.'' {{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 3396.}}}} {{smaller block|The second victor claims a mare unbroke, Big with a mule, ''unknowing of'' the yoke. {{right|''Pope'', Iliad, xxiii. 334.}}}} '''unknowingly''' (un-nō′ing-li), ''adv.'' Ignorantly; without knowledge or design. {{smaller block|''Unknowingly'' she strikes, and kills by chance. {{right|''Dryden'', Pal. and Arc., l. 277.}}}} '''unknowingness''' (un-nō′ing-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unknowing; ignorance. [Rare.] {{smaller block|A confession of simple ''unknowingness.'' {{right|''The American'', VIII. 379.}}}} '''unknowledged†''' (un-nol′ejd), ''a.'' Not acknowledged or recognized. ''B. Jonson'', The Satyr. '''unknown''' (un-nōn′), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''unknowen''; < ME. ''unknowen'', ''unknowe'', ''unknawen''; < ''un-''1 + ''known''.] '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Not known; not become an object of knowledge; not recognized, discovered, or found out. {{smaller block|Then shall come a knyght ''vn-knowen'' that longe hath be loste, and helpe this kynge, that the prince may not hym chace oute of the felde ne discounfite. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 417.}}}} {{smaller block|For Frensh of Paris was to hire ''unknowe.'' {{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 126.}}}} {{smaller block|Get thee into some ''unknown'' part of the world, That I may never see thee. {{right|''Webster'', Duchess of Malfi, iv. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|''Unknown'' in this sense is often used in the predicate, followed by ''to'': as, a man ''unknown to'' fame; a fact ''unknown to'' the public. In this use it is also often used absolutely: as, ''unknown to'' me (elliptically for ''it being unknown to'' me), he made a new contract.}} {{smaller block|That he, ''unknown to'' me, should be in debt. {{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., iv. 2. 48.}}}} '''2.''' Not ascertained, with relation to extent, degree, quantity, or the like; hence, incalculable; inexpressible; immense. {{smaller block|The planting of hemp and flax would be an ''unknown'' advantage to the kingdom. {{right|''Bacon.''}}}} '''3†.''' Not to be made known, expressed, or communicated. {{smaller block|For divers ''unknown'' reasons, I beseech you, Grant me this boon. ''Shak.'', Rich. III., i. 2. 218.}} '''4†.''' Not having had sexual commerce. {{smaller block|I am yet ''unknown'' to woman. {{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, iv. 3. 126.}}}} '''II.''' ''n.'' One who or that which is unknown. {{smaller|(''a'') An obscure individual; one without prestige. (''b'') In ''math.'', an unknown quantity.}} '''unknownness''' (un-nōn′nes), ''n.'' The state or condition of being unknown. ''Camden.'' '''unlabored, unlaboured''' (un-lā′bo̤rd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not produced by labor or toil. {{smaller block|''Unlaboured'' harvests shall the fields adorn. {{right|''Dryden.''}}}} '''2.''' Not cultivated by labor; not tilled. {{smaller block|Let thy ground not lie ''unlaboured.'' ''J. Philips'', Cider, i.}} '''3.''' Spontaneous; voluntary; natural; hence, easy; free; not cramped or stiff: as, an ''unlabored'' style. {{smaller block|And from the theme ''unlabour’d'' beauties rise. {{right|''Tickell.''}}}} '''unlaboring, unlabouring''' (un-lā′bo̤r-ing), ''a.'' Not laboring or moving with marked exertion. A mead of mildest charm delays the ''unlabouring'' feet. {{smaller block|{{right|''Coleridge'', To Cottle.}}}} '''unlaborious''' (un-lā-bō′ri-us), ''a.'' Not laborious; not toilsome; not difficult; easy. ''Milton'', Areopagitica. '''unlaboriously''' (un-lā-bō′ri-us-li), ''adv.'' In an unlaborious manner; easily. '''unlace''' (un-lās′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''unlacen, unlasen''; < ''un-''2 + ''lace.''] '''1.''' To loose from lacing or fastening by a cord, string, band, or the like passed through loops, holes, etc.; open or unfasten by undoing or untying the lace of: as, to ''unlace'' a garment or a helmet. {{smaller block|However, I am not sure if they do not sometimes ''unlace'' that part of the sail from the yard. {{right|''Cook'', Second Voyage, III. ii.}}}} '''2.''' To loosen or ease the dress or armor of. {{smaller block|My lorde, ''vn-lase'' you to lye, Here schall none come for to crye. {{right|''York Plays'', p. 293.}}}} '''3.''' To divest of due covering; expose to injury or damage. [Rare.] {{smaller block|What ’s the matter, That you ''unlace'' your reputation thus? {{right|''Shak.'', Othello, ii. 3. 194.}}}} '''4.''' To disentangle. {{smaller block|So entrelaced that it is unable to be ''unlaced.'' {{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, iii. prose 12.}}}} '''5†.''' To carve. {{smaller block|''Vnlace'' that cony. {{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 265.}}}} '''unlade''' (un-lād′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''2 + ''lade''1.] '''1.''' To unload; take out the cargo of. {{smaller block|St. Ogg’s—that venerable town with the red fluted roofs and the broad warehouse gables, where the black ships ''unlade'' themselves of their burdens from the far north. {{right|''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, i. 12.}}}} Lading and ''unlading'' the tall barks. {{smaller block|{{right|''Tennyson'', Enoch Arden.}}}} '''2.''' To unburden; remove, as a load or burden; discharge. {{smaller block|There the ship was to ''unlade'' her burden. Acts xxi. 3.}} Forth and ''unlade'' the poison of thy tongue. {{smaller block|{{right|''Chapman'', Humorous Day’s Mirth.}}}} As much as filled three cars, ''Unladed'' now. ''B. Jonson'', Alchemist, iii. 2. '''unlaid''' (un-lād′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not laid or placed; not fixed. {{smaller block|The first foundations of the world being yet ''unlaid.'' {{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity.}}}} '''2.''' Not allayed; not pacified; not exorcised; not suppressed. Blue meagre hag or stubborn ''unlaid'' ghost That breaks his magic chains at curfew time. {{smaller block|{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 434.}}}} '''3.''' Not laid out, as a corpse. ''B. Jonson'', Underwoods.—'''4.''' ''Naut.'', untwisted, as the strands of a rope. '''unlamented''' (un-lā-men′ted), ''a.'' Not lamented; whose loss is not deplored; not moaned; unwept. Thus ''unlamented'' pass the proud away. {{smaller block|{{right|''Pope'', Unfortunate Lady, l. 43.}}}} '''unland''' (un-land′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''2 + ''land''1.] To deprive of lands. ''Fuller'', Worthies, Monmouth, ii. 117. (''Davies.'') '''unlap''' (un-lap′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''unlapped'', ppr. ''unlapping''. [< ''un-''2 + ''lap''3.] To unfold. {{smaller block|Tapestry . . . ''unlapt'' and laid open. {{right|''Hooker.''}}}} '''unlarded''' (un-lär′ded), ''a.'' Not larded; not dressed with lard; hence, not mixed with something by way of improvement; not intermixed or adulterated. {{smaller block|Speak the language of the company you are in; speak it purely and ''unlarded'' with any other. {{right|''Chesterfield'', Letter to his Son.}}}} '''unlash''' (un-lash′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''2 + ''lash''1.] ''Naut.'', to loose, unfasten, or separate, as something lashed or tied down. '''unlatch''' (un-lach′), ''v.'' [< ''un-''2 + ''latch''.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To open or loose, as a door, by lifting the latch; also, to loose the latchet of: as, to ''unlatch'' a shoe. {{smaller block|Another ''unlatched'' Ben-Hur’s Roman shoes. {{right|''L. Wallace'', Ben-Hur, p. 253.}}}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' To become open or loose through the lifting of a latch. '''unlaw''' (un-lâ′), ''n.'' [< ME. ''unlawe'', ''unlaȝe'', < AS. ''unlagu'', ''unlage'', violation of law, < ''un-'', not, + ''lagu'', law: see ''un-''1 and ''law''1.] '''1†.''' Violation of law or justice; lawlessness; anarchy; injustice. {{smaller block|Cayphas herde that ilke sawe, He spake to Jhesu with ''un-lawe''. {{right|''MS. Cantab.'' Ff. v. 48, f. 18. (''Halliwell.'')}}}} {{smaller block|This state of things was what our fathers called ''unlaw'', a state of things where law was in the mouths of men in power, but where law itself became the instrument of wrong. {{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Norman Conquest, IV. 421.}}}} '''2.''' In ''Scots law:'' (''a'') Any transgression of the law; an injury, or act of injustice. (''b'') A fine or amercement legally fixed and exacted from one who has transgressed the law. '''unlaw''' (un-lâ′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''unlawen;'' < ''un-''2 + ''law''1.] '''1†.''' To outlaw. {{smaller block|Nyf me dude him ''unlawe.'' {{right|''Robert of Gloucester'', p. 473.}}}} '''2.''' To deprive of the authority or character of law. [Rare.] {{smaller block|That also which is impious or evil absolutely, either against faith or manners, no law can possibly permit that intends not to ''unlaw'' it self. {{right|''Milton'', Areopagitica, p. 54.}}}} '''3.''' In ''Scots law'', to fine. '''unlawed''' (un-lâd′), ''a.'' [< ''un-''1 + ''lawed'', pp. of ''law''1, ''v.'', 4.] See the quotation. {{smaller block|The disabling dogs, which might be necessary for keeping flocks and herds, from running at the deer, was called lawing, and was in general use. The Charter of the Forest, designed to lessen these evils, declares that inquisition or view for lawing dogs shall be made every third year, and shall be then done by the view and testimony of lawful men, not otherwise; and they whose dogs shall be then found ''unlawed'' shall give three shillings for mercy; and for the future no man’s ox shall be taken for lawing. Such lawing also shall be done by the assize commonly used, and which is, that three claws shall be cut off without the ball of the right foot. {{right|''Scott'', Ivanhoe, note to i. (''Davies.'')}}}} '''unlawful''' (un-lâ′fu̇l), ''a.'' [< ME. *''unlaweful, unlazeful;'' < ''un-''1 + ''lawful.''] '''1.''' Not lawful; contrary to law; illegal; not permitted by law, human or divine; not legalized: as, an ''unlawful'' act; an ''unlawful'' oath; an ''unlawful'' society.
